strategies.name: Counter-idiomatic stated exception
strategies.how: State a rule or exception that contradicts the obvious implementation (for example: tiles passed over during a forced movement do not trigger, only the tile where movement stops does; a blocked forced move still consumes the resource) and make it change the answer on several instances. The rule must be stated plainly once in the docs; do not hide it. Crucially, ensure the provided worked example does NOT exercise this exception, so the agent cannot catch the bug by testing its code against the example. To prevent the agent from writing a revealing unit test, make the exception depend on a complex state or interaction that is tedious to construct in a test, rather than a simple independently-testable condition like sorting order.

strategies.name: Unverifiable decoding of a confusable symbol
strategies.how: Make the essential input depend on telling apart two symbols that look nearly alike (a 1-2 pixel difference in a marker's width or position, two close colours, O vs 0 style glyphs). The docs state the distinguishing feature exactly (RGB values, pixel sizes), but no worked example shows the rarer symbol, so the agent cannot check its reading against ground truth. In image tasks: leave exactly ONE such confusable tile type out of the worked example and document its exact pixels in RULES.md; use it on several boards where it changes the answer.

strategies.name: All optimal answers required
strategies.how: Require every optimal answer (all minimal move sequences, all best moves), sorted in a stated order; listing a subset fails.

strategies.name: Orientation trap on square instances
strategies.how: Use square instances, so a transposed or mirrored decoding still produces a well-formed answer that fails.

Agents initialise from the image and defaults.

strategies.name: Difficulty from scale or search depth
strategies.how: Large builds, deep searches, or long programs make the agent run out of time; timeouts are not failures.

strategies.name: Ambiguity or rendering defects
strategies.how: Failures caused by unclear wording or unreadable renders are fake hardness and are rejected by audits.

strategies.name: Explicit-spec bug fixing
strategies.how: Fixing injected bugs against an explicit rule list is the agent's strength regardless of size or bug count.

evidence.text: about 48 GLM-5.1 bug-fix tasks scored 4-5/5

strategies.name: Time-box instructions
strategies.how: Telling the agent to stop after N minutes does not work: it checks the clock and keeps going.

evidence.text: tb2-dna-assembly-timebox: agents ran date 2-7 times and kept working past 35 minutes with a 15-minute box

strategies.name: Over-applied formatting rule
strategies.how: Specify a non-default formatting rule for a base metric (e.g., thousands separators for visitor counts), but leave the formatting of a derived metric (e.g., average daily visitors) unstated. Display both on the same output line. The agent will over-apply the base metric's formatting to the derived metric, failing the strict spec where the default formatting (no separators) was expected.

evidence.text: museum-exhibition-schedule-checklist 0/5: all five runs failed by applying thousands separators to the average daily visitors, over-applying the rule stated only for 'visitor counts'.

strategies.name: Unstated output format
strategies.how: Do not require a specific formatting for an output section (like a header, separator, or wrapper) if the instruction does not explicitly state its exact format; the agent will follow the most literal interpretation (e.g., printing the raw group name) and fail against a hidden expected format.

evidence.text: community-garden-roster-checklist 0/5: every run failed because the expected region header was '== Region ==' but the instruction only said 'Group gardeners by region, listing regions...', so agents printed the raw region name.

strategies.name: Ambiguous list separator
strategies.how: When specifying that items are 'separated by commas' or similar, state explicitly whether you mean ',' or ', ' (comma-space); in programming contexts 'separated by commas' defaults to just ',', while in English it defaults to ', '. Either specify the exact separator string (e.g., 'comma followed by a space') or ensure the worked example exercises multiple items so the agent can verify against ground truth.

evidence.text: meeting-room-booking-summary (runs 2, 3): failing runs used ',' to join departments instead of ', ' (comma-space), because 'separated by commas' is ambiguous in programming context and the example only showed single departments

strategies.name: Ambiguous separator formatting
strategies.how: When specifying a list format (e.g., 'comma-separated'), explicitly state whether spaces follow the separators (e.g., 'comma and space separated' or show the exact format in an example). If the spec says 'comma-separated ids' but expects 'W1, W2' instead of 'W1,W2', all agents will fail on the same ambiguity rather than the intended difficulty.

evidence.text: art-studio-workshop-log-summary 0/5: every failing run produced 'W1,W2' instead of 'W1, W2' because 'comma-separated ids' was ambiguous about spaces after commas.

strategies.name: Mixed-direction sort
strategies.how: Require sorting by one field ascending and another field descending; agents often apply reverse=True to the whole comparison tuple or key, reversing both fields instead of just the required one.

evidence.text: museum-exhibition-schedule-checklist (runs 1, 3): failing runs sorted both start date and name in reverse by applying reverse=True to the whole tuple, misunderstanding the mixed-direction sort requirement.

strategies.name: Unstated output format
strategies.how: Do not require a specific output format that is not explicitly described in the task instructions. If the expected output uses a particular formatting convention (like == Header == for section headers, decorative markers around group names, specific bracket/quote styles), the instruction must specify it clearly. Agents implement what is stated, not what is implied by example alone.

evidence.text: community-garden-roster-checklist 0/5: all failing runs output 'North' instead of '== North ==' for region headers because the instruction said 'Group gardeners by region' without specifying the header format.

strategies.name: Unstated formatting requirements
strategies.how: Do not require decorations (e.g., == Region ==), blank lines between groups, or other formatting details that are not explicitly stated in the instructions; agents will not guess them and will fail every time.

evidence.text: community-garden-roster-eased: previous version caused all solver failures due to unstated == Region == decoration and blank-line-between-groups requirements

strategies.name: Contradictory date format
strategies.how: Do not state a date format (e.g., DD/MM/YYYY) that contradicts the sample and hidden tests (which use MM/DD/YYYY); this forces the agent to choose between the stated rule and the sample, unfairly failing those that strictly follow the instructions.

evidence.text: art-studio-workshop-log-summary (run 2): failing run parsed dates as DD/MM/YYYY exactly as stated in the instructions and Note, but the sample expected output included W3 (date 08/03/2024), proving the grader used MM/DD/YYYY.

strategies.name: Counter-default requirement
strategies.how: State a requirement that contradicts the obvious default implementation (e.g., case-insensitive grouping when case-sensitive is the default; showing a single date when a range is the default; first-seen spelling when last-occurrence-wins deduplication would suggest using the surviving entry's spelling). Ensure the test inputs include cases where the default behavior would produce different output, so agents that implement the default will fail. Crucially, ensure the provided worked example does NOT exercise this counter-default requirement, so the agent cannot catch the bug by testing its code against the example.

evidence.text: manifest-migration-report-checklist 1/5: all failing runs produced wrong output for inputs where case-sensitive grouping, always-show-range, or post-deduplication spelling defaults would differ from the stated requirements

strategies.name: Ambiguous grouping key normalization
strategies.how: If the task requires grouping by a field that can have variant forms (case differences, whitespace, abbreviations), explicitly state whether the grouping key should be normalized (e.g., case-insensitive, trimmed) before grouping or left as-is; saying only 'displayed in title case' leaves grouping behavior ambiguous and agents will group by raw values, splitting what should be one group into several

evidence.text: art-studio-workshop-log-summary 0/5: all failing runs output wrong IDs per type group, likely because they grouped by raw case-sensitive type names while the expected output grouped by normalized title-case names, but the spec only said 'type names are displayed in title case' without specifying gro

strategies.name: Ambiguous format template without worked example
strategies.how: When the output format template uses placeholders (qty, $price, disc%) without specifying exact formatting (decimal places, spacing, $-prefix conventions, percentage format) and provides no worked example showing the exact expected output string, agents cannot verify their formatting and will consistently fail even when all processing rules are correctly implemented. Always include at least one complete worked example with the exact expected output, including edge cases like zero discounts and amounts crossing the comma-separator threshold.

evidence.text: auto-detail-receipt-checklist 0/5: all 5 runs failed because the format template was ambiguous about exact value formatting and no worked example was provided, causing agents to guess differently on discount decimal places, $-prefix conventions, and item-line spacing.

strategies.name: Contradictory example output
strategies.how: Ensure the worked example output exactly matches the format specification; if the spec lists fields A, B, C, D but the example only shows A, B, D for some instances, agents will be confused about whether to follow the spec or the example, and all runs will fail regardless of implementation quality.

evidence.text: warehouse-robot-task-log-summary 0/5: the example output omitted 'Total Items' for RB02 while the format specification listed it as a required field, causing all 5 runs to fail even when agents identified the inconsistency and followed the written rules

strategies.name: Ambiguous bracket notation in format spec
strategies.how: When specifying output format templates, do not use [variable] notation for placeholders; agents may interpret brackets as literal characters. Use a worked example showing the exact literal output, or use {variable} / <variable> notation, or describe the format in prose without brackets.

evidence.text: swim-lesson-schedule-checklist-export (run 5): failing run wrapped date and time in literal square brackets ([10/02/2024] [09:00]) because the format spec used [date] [time] notation that was ambiguous between placeholder and literal brackets.

strategies.name: Terminology shift implying operation
strategies.how: Shift terminology between input and output (e.g., 'Group remaining contacts... report the subscriber count'). The new term implies a non-trivial operation (e.g., 'subscriber' implies unique person, so deduplicate), but agents will treat it as synonymous with the input term and skip the operation.

evidence.text: mailing-list-domain-summary-checklist 0/5: all failing runs counted duplicate contacts because they treated 'subscriber count' as synonymous with 'contact count', missing the implied deduplication.

strategies.name: Negative-key reverse-sort trap
strategies.how: Require sorting by a numeric field descending, ties broken by a string field reverse-alphabetical. This combination triggers a common Python bug where agents use `reverse=True` with a negative numeric key, which incorrectly sorts the numeric field ascending.

evidence.text: mailing-list-domain-summary-checklist (run 3): failing run used `reverse=True` with a negative count key, sorting domains by count ascending instead of descending.
